title: SELECT, FROM, aliases, and reading a table
objective: Read any table, choose exactly the columns you need, compute new columns, and name every output column deliberately with AS.
context: Every analysis starts with 'what is actually in this table?'. The merchandising team wants quick lists — supplier directory, price sheet, order-line values — and each list must have clean, predictable column names so it can be pasted into a report or fed into a dashboard.

exercises.title: Supplier directory
exercises.question: Procurement wants the full supplier directory.
exercises.prompt: Return every supplier with columns supplier_id, supplier_name, country.
hints: All rows, three named columns — no filtering needed.
SELECT col_a, col_b, col_c FROM table;
SELECT supplier_id, supplier_name, country FROM suppliers;
exercises.why: Listing columns explicitly (instead of SELECT *) makes reports stable when someone adds a column to the table later.

recall.q: Which clause does the database logically evaluate first: SELECT or FROM?
recall.a: FROM — it first decides where rows come from, then SELECT shapes them.

exercises.title: Customer contact sheet with clean column names
exercises.question: Customer success wants a contact sheet whose headers read customer_name and email_address.
exercises.prompt: Return all customers with columns customer_id, customer_name (from name) and email_address (from email). Keep NULL emails as they are.
hints: SELECT customer_id, name AS customer_name, email AS email_address FROM customers;
exercises.why: Downstream tools match on column names. Aliasing is how you control the contract between your query and whoever consumes it.

recall.q: Is the AS keyword required for a column alias in most SQL dialects?
recall.a: No — `name customer_name` also works — but writing AS is clearer and is the habit to keep.

exercises.title: Price sheet with tax
exercises.question: Finance needs each product's list price and the price including 8% sales tax.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, list_price and price_with_tax (list_price * 1.08 rounded to 2 decimals) for every product.
hints: A computed column is just an expression in the SELECT list.
exercises.why: Derived columns are the bread and butter of analytics. Notice product 19 has a NULL list price, so its taxed price is NULL too — arithmetic with NULL is NULL.

recall.a: NULL. Any arithmetic with NULL yields NULL.

exercises.title: Order line totals
exercises.question: What is the value of every order line?
exercises.prompt: Return order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price and line_total (quantity * unit_price) for all 150 order lines.
hints: Select the five original columns plus the computed line_total.
exercises.why: Revenue in this warehouse is always quantity × unit_price at line level — the list price in products is NOT what the customer paid (discounts!).

recall.q: Why compute revenue from order_items.unit_price instead of products.list_price?
recall.a: Because unit_price is the price actually charged (after discounts); list_price is just the catalog price.

exercises.title: Table alias and a combined label
exercises.question: The CRM import needs one text label per customer like 'Alice Johnson (North)'.
exercises.prompt: Using the table alias c, return c.customer_id as customer_id and a column customer_label built as name || ' (' || region || ')'. (Customers with a NULL region will get a NULL label — that is expected here; Lesson 3 fixes it.)
hints: FROM customers AS c lets you write c.name, c.region.
exercises.why: Table aliases become essential with joins (Module 2). Seeing NULL poison a concatenation now will make COALESCE click in Lesson 3.

recall.a: NULL. (Snowflake's CONCAT also returns NULL; use COALESCE or CONCAT_WS-style handling.)

exercises.title: Refund ledger with literal columns
exercises.question: Accounting wants refunds as negative ledger entries tagged with a transaction type.
exercises.prompt: Return return_id, return_date, a literal column transaction_type with the value 'refund', and signed_amount = the refund_amount as a negative number.
hints: You can SELECT a constant: 'refund' AS transaction_type.
Negate with a minus sign: -refund_amount (or refund_amount * -1).
SELECT return_id, return_date, 'refund' AS transaction_type, -refund_amount AS signed_amount FROM returns;
exercises.why: Literal columns are how you label rows before stacking datasets together with UNION ALL (Lesson 25).

recall.q: How do you add a constant column to every row of a result?
recall.a: Put the literal in the SELECT list with an alias, e.g. 'refund' AS transaction_type.

worked_example.question: Show each product's name, category and price, plus a 10%-off sale price.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT p.product_name,
       p.category,
       p.list_price,
       ROUND(p.list_price * 0.9, 2) AS sale_price
FROM products AS p
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: `p` is a table alias; `sale_price` is a column alias. `ROUND(..., 2)` keeps currency readable. Note `LIMIT 5` only trims the preview — remove it to see all 25 products.

recipe:
**Recipe: read a table in 4 moves**

1. `FROM table` — decide *where* the rows come from (read this clause first, even though it is written second).
2. `SELECT col1, col2` — pick only the columns you need. `SELECT *` is for exploring, not for reports.
3. Compute: `quantity * unit_price`, `ROUND(x, 2)`, `a || ' ' || b` (string concat). Any expression works.
4. Name it: `expression AS clean_name`. Table aliases (`FROM products AS p`, then `p.list_price`) keep
   longer queries readable and become mandatory once you join tables.

```sql
SELECT p.product_name,
       ROUND(p.list_price * 0.9, 2) AS sale_price
FROM   products AS p;
```

**Logical order of evaluation:** `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`.
That's why an alias defined in SELECT can't be used in WHERE (later lessons), but can in ORDER BY.

**NULL preview:** any arithmetic or `||` with NULL yields NULL. You'll handle that properly in Lesson 3.
common_mistakes: Leaving computed columns unnamed — you get a header like `quantity * unit_price` that breaks downstream tools.
Using `SELECT *` in a final report: it silently changes when the table changes.
Using double quotes for text. In standard SQL 'single quotes' are strings and "double quotes" are identifiers.
Assuming list_price is what the customer paid — always use order_items.unit_price for revenue.
Forgetting that NULL in arithmetic or concatenation makes the whole expression NULL.
recall: Write the logical evaluation order of a SELECT query.
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
What's the difference between a table alias and a column alias?
A table alias (FROM products AS p) names a table so you can write p.col; a column alias (expr AS name) names an output column.
Which quote style marks a string literal?
